A bouquet is real in the Indian flower trade but sits fourth on the list — jasmine is documented for garlands, bouquets, decorating the hair of women and religious offerings, in that order.

faqs.question: Can I send flowers to my wife on the actual day of the wedding?
faqs.answer: You can, but the ceremony flowers are almost never yours to send — a decorator has already been booked for the garlands and the venue. If you want something that is specifically from you, send it the morning before, or after the event, when she is reachable and the garlands have finished their two days.

faqs.question: How long will a wedding garland stay fresh?
faqs.answer: Plan on about two days. A 2023 ICAR-IIHR evaluation of a tuberose selection judged good for garland preparation records a shelf life of two days under ambient conditions, and the follow-up shelf-life study ran its trials at 32±1°C room temperature.

faqs.question: Is jasmine or tuberose better for a garland?
faqs.answer: Both are documented garland flowers and they do different jobs. Jasmine is described in the research as used for garlands, for decorating the hair of women and for religious offerings, and carries maximum fragrance when fully open; tuberose is the white weight, valued for floral ornaments, artistic garlands and buttonholes.

faqs.question: What flowers can she wear in her hair?
faqs.answer: Jasmine is the flower the literature actually names for this. The Journal of Extension Education's study of jasmine growers in Tirunelveli lists "decorating hair of women" as one of its standard uses alongside garlands and religious offerings.

faqs.question: Is it odd to give my wife her own flowers when the venue is already full of them?
faqs.answer: No, because they are two different gifts. The venue flowers and the garlands are public and arranged by someone else; anything you hand her directly is private and read that way, which is the distinction research on gift-giving in marital rites keeps returning to.

faqs.question: Which flowers should I avoid at an Indian wedding?
faqs.answer: We could not source an answer to this and will not invent one. Confident lists of forbidden wedding flowers circulate widely without citations, and regional practice varies enough that the only reliable source is the family and the decorator you are working with.

faqs.question: What do I do if the flowers turn up wilted on the morning?
faqs.answer: Assume it will happen to some of them and order accordingly. Loose flowers are highly perishable and the published shelf-life work on tuberose exists precisely because room-temperature storage in Indian conditions is hard, so buy buds that are opening rather than already open, and buy the same morning.

faqs.question: How far ahead should I order wedding flowers?
faqs.answer: Book the florist or decorator weeks ahead, but have the flowers themselves cut for the morning of. The two-day holding time means anything delivered earlier is spending its shelf life sitting in a room rather than on the two of you.

faqs.question: My wedding is in a city I do not live in — how do I arrange her flowers?
faqs.answer: Use a florist in the wedding city, not a national delivery service, and hand the timing to whoever is already on the ground. Loose flowers do not travel well, which is the whole reason post-harvest research on them is a live field in India.

faqs.question: What should I write on the card that goes with her flowers?
faqs.answer: Write the thing you would not say in front of two hundred people. The flowers themselves are the public gesture; the card is the only part of it that is addressed to one person, so specificity beats formality every time.

faqs.question: What happens to the garlands after the ceremony?
faqs.answer: They are finished within roughly two days, which is what the published shelf-life figure for garland-grade tuberose describes. Whole fields of post-harvest research exist to stretch that window with packaging and preservatives, and it still ends in days — so if you want something she keeps, it has to be a different object.

faqs.question: Do flowers still matter for a small registry wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the garland often survives even when everything else is stripped back, because it is the part two people do to each other rather than something staged around them. A single jasmine strand for her hair does more work at a small ceremony than a large arrangement.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Flowers for Wife on Wedding Day, and Where a Bouquet Fits

Flowers for your wife on the wedding day, at an Indian wedding, are mostly not a bouquet. Indian horticultural research describes the flowers of a ceremony as *loose* flowers: tuberose grown and graded specifically for [garland preparation](https://jhs.iihr.res.in/index.php/jhs/article/view/2148), jasmine used for [garlands, for decorating the hair of women and for religious offerings](https://www.extensioneducation.org/index.php/jee/article/view/75).

A tuberose selection judged suitable for garlands held **two days at ambient temperature**. A bouquet is a genuine product of that trade — both papers list it — but it sits on a list where the garland comes first.

We build the thing that outlasts the flowers: **801 digital bouquet pages, 23.4% of all 3,417 pages** made here since 2026-03-12, and **50.2% of shared pages are opened on a phone**.

Search flowers for wife on wedding day and you get ten shops. Below instead: what each flower does on the day, whether you mean the wedding or the anniversary, and the part we cannot do for you.

## What are wedding day flowers for a bride in India?

Wedding day flowers for a bride in India are predominantly loose flowers — individual blooms sold by weight and assembled on the day into garlands and hair ornaments — rather than a wrapped, wired bouquet carried down an aisle. The flower reaches the bride already made into something she wears.

That is not a stylistic observation, it is how the crop is bred and graded. The Journal of Horticultural Sciences evaluation of tuberose genotype IIHR 17-23SP-08 reports a loose flower yield of 18.88 tonnes per hectare per year and assesses the genotype's fitness by whether it is [suitable as a loose flower for garland preparation](https://jhs.iihr.res.in/index.php/jhs/article/view/2148).

Garland suitability is a breeding target. Nobody breeds a tuberose for aisle-carrying.

## Do you mean the wedding day, or the wedding anniversary?

Settle this before you order anything, because the autocomplete for this phrase mixes both and the two need opposite things. "Wedding day" means the day of the ceremony: you are one of the two people in it, you are not reachable, and the flowers are being handled by a decorator you have never met. Under that constraint the two-day holding time reported for garland tuberose in 2023 is the whole plan — order for the morning of, or not at all.

A wedding anniversary is the reverse: an ordinary working day, one recipient, and a delivery slot you control. Everything below is about the ceremony. If you want the anniversary answer, this is not that page, and the honest version is that anniversary flowers are a solved problem — any florist takes a morning slot.

## Which flowers for a wedding, and what each one is documented to do

We only list what a source we read actually states. Each entry gives the source, the documented use, the holding time the source reports, and what to do with that.

### 1. Jasmine — garlands, hair and offerings

*Jasminum sambac* is described in the Journal of Extension Education's study of 120 growers in Vallioor block, Tirunelveli, as one of the oldest fragrant flowers cultivated by man, used for [making garlands, bouquets, decorating the hair of women and religious offerings](https://www.extensioneducation.org/index.php/jee/article/view/75). On the day it goes into the garland and into her hair — what most families simply call a gajra, though we could not source that word itself to a scholarly work. Holding time: neither paper we read gives a figure for jasmine.

Chemical Engineering Transactions separately records that jasmine [plays an important role in religious offerings and social and cultural activities of India](https://www.cetjournal.it/index.php/cet/article/view/5297) and that fully open flowers carry maximum fragrance. What to do with that: buy it opening, not open, and buy it the same morning.

### 2. Tuberose — garlands with a two-day clock

Tuberose, *Agave amica*, is valued for [floral ornaments, bouquets, artistic garlands, buttonholes and essential oil](https://jhs.iihr.res.in/index.php/jhs/article/view/1851). On the day it is the white weight in a garland.

Holding time is the number that should change your planning: the IIHR 17-23SP-08 evaluation, published June 2023, records a shelf life of two days under ambient conditions for loose flowers used in garlands, and the 2024 shelf-life study ran its storage trials at a room temperature of 32±1°C — which is what a September afternoon in most of India actually is. What to do with that: the garland is a two-day object at best, so order for the morning of, and stop imagining it as a keepsake.

### 3. Marigold and rose — used everywhere, sourced nowhere we could find

Marigold and rose are visibly everywhere at Indian weddings. We could not find an open-access, peer-reviewed source that documents their specific role on a wedding day, as opposed to their production economics, and we are not going to assert one from memory. Holding time: unknown to us.

What to do with that: ask your decorator, and treat any blog that gives you confident marigold symbolism without a citation — including this one, had we done it — as a guess.

### 4. The bouquet — a real product, a smaller role

Here is where the usual advice gets it backwards. Every result that ranks for this phrase assumes the question is which bouquet to order. But the bouquet appears in our sources as one entry in a list — jasmine is used for "garlands, bouquets, decorating the hair of women"; tuberose for "floral ornaments, bouquets, artistic garlands, buttonholes." It is real, and it is fourth or fifth on the list.

Holding time: not stated in either paper. What to do with that: buy the bouquet if you want it, but do not buy it believing it is the flower that matters that day.

## Bouquet for wedding versus garland: what the numbers say

This compares the four things you are actually choosing between, using only figures the source states.

| Option | Documented use | Holding time in the source | SubhSandesh measurement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tuberose loose flowers | Garland preparation (JHS, 2023) | 2 days at ambient temperature | Not measured — we do not sell flowers |
| Jasmine loose flowers | Garlands, bouquets, hair, religious offerings (JEE, 2016) | Not stated in the paper | Not measured — we do not sell flowers |
| Cut bouquet from a florist | Floral ornaments, bouquets, artistic garlands, buttonholes (JHS, 2024) | Not stated in the paper | Not measured — we do not sell flowers |
| A digital bouquet page | A link she opens; nothing to keep alive | No expiry | 801 built, 23.4% of 3,417 pages; 12.3 views each |

The takeaway is the last column read honestly: on three of four rows we have nothing to offer, because a florist can do something we cannot.

## When a link is the wrong answer on a wedding day

On the day of the ceremony, real flowers are not optional and a link cannot stand in for them. The garland is a physical object two people put over each other's heads in front of everyone they know. Flowers in her hair are worn.

Neither has a digital form, and any page that suggests otherwise is selling you something.

Every florist in the search results for this phrase can deliver something we cannot deliver at all. If you have one decision to make and it is flowers for the ceremony, close this page and call a florist in the city the wedding is in, this week.

There is a second case where we lose. Our own data says 50.2% of shared pages are opened on a phone — so the whole thing assumes she has a phone in her hand. On a wedding day she will not, for most of the day, and it will be in someone else's bag.

## What we would actually send, and when

The gap worth filling is not the ceremony, it is the twenty-four hours around it — the morning before she is handed over to a schedule, and the week after, when the garlands have finished their two days and gone.

That is where a page earns its place. Our [Build-a-Bouquet page](https://subhsandesh.in/bouquet-gf) hand-ties twelve blooms into an arrangement with a card attached, and it is the second most-made thing on the site: 801 pages, 23.4% of everything created here. It does not wilt in a September afternoon, and it averages 12.3 views per page, which mostly means it gets reopened.

For something plainer and less flower-shaped, the [I love you page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) is the most-made template we have. If the invitation itself is still unsent, the [Hindu wedding invitation page](https://subhsandesh.in/wedding-shaadi) is a separate template.

Two practical notes from our own numbers. Give yourself time: the median gap between a creator's first save and last edit is 6.9 hours, sampled across 1,001 pages, so this is not a five-minute job the morning of. And 42.7% of creators password-protect the page before sharing it — 1,458 of 3,417 — which on a wedding day, when half the family will be looking over her shoulder, is worth doing.

One more honest note. Research on gift-giving in contemporary marital rites describes a real tension between reciprocity and [conspicuous, prestigious consumption](https://www.eap-iea.org/index.php/eap/article/view/578) — the study is of a rural European setting, not India, so we will not stretch it. But the mechanism it names is familiar at any wedding: what gets given in front of an audience and what gets given privately are two different gifts.

Flowers on the day are the public one. Send the private one separately.

## Sources

- Journal of Horticultural Sciences, 18(1), 30 June 2023 — [evaluation of tuberose genotype IIHR 17-23SP-08](https://jhs.iihr.res.in/index.php/jhs/article/view/2148): loose flower yield 18.88 t/ha/year; suitable as a loose flower for garland preparation with a shelf life of two days under ambient conditions.
- Journal of Horticultural Sciences, 19(1), 30 June 2024 — [shelf-life extension of tuberose flowers](https://jhs.iihr.res.in/index.php/jhs/article/view/1851): tuberose valued for floral ornaments, bouquets, artistic garlands, buttonholes and essential oil; storage trials at 32±1°C.
- Journal of Extension Education, 28(1), 21 November 2016 — [technology adoption behaviour of jasmine growers](https://www.extensioneducation.org/index.php/jee/article/view/75): jasmine used for making garlands, bouquets, decorating hair of women and religious offerings; 120 growers sampled in Vallioor block, Tirunelveli.
- Chemical Engineering Transactions, 40, 20 September 2014 — [volatile aroma compounds of Indian jasmine](https://www.cetjournal.it/index.php/cet/article/view/5297): jasmine is an important commercial traditional flower crop of India with a role in religious offerings and social and cultural activities.
- Etnoantropološki problemi, 8(2), 29 August 2013 — [gift giving and consumption in contemporary marital rites](https://www.eap-iea.org/index.php/eap/article/view/578): reciprocity and conspicuous consumption as competing forms in wedding gift exchange.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page in this SERP that answers the question with Indian horticultural research instead of a bridal-bouquet listicle: tuberose bred and graded for garland preparation, a two-day holding time under ambient conditions, and jasmine documented for garlands and for decorating the hair of women — none of which appears in the top ten, where nine of ten results are product grids and the one reachable editorial page (Teleflora) is entirely Western bridal-bouquet framing. Three cultural claims in the batch brief could not be sourced and are therefore absent from the page: that the garland exchange is called varmala or jaimala (no open-access scholarly source found for either term — DOAJ returns 0 for "varmala", "jaimala" and "malai maatral"); that the mandap's floral decor is documented anywhere citable (DOAJ "mandap"/"mandapa" returns only temple architecture and a Yagya-mandap construction paper); and that a Hindu wedding has no bridal bouquet at all — which my own sources actively contradict, since both the jasmine and the tuberose papers list "bouquets" among standard uses. The page says the bouquet is real but fourth on the list, which is what the sources support, and it names marigold and rose as unsourced in a dedicated H3 rather than asserting symbolism. Two further gaps: the strongest number for this angle — India's 2024-25 split of 3,226.20 thousand tonnes of loose flowers against 1,039.29 thousand tonnes of cut flowers — sits on apeda.gov.in/floriculture, which USED-SOURCES.md records as already spent, and the equivalent figure could not be obtained from a clean domain (nhb.gov.in is session-locked, midh.gov.in and agriwelfare.gov.in PDFs return 403). All five citations were verified from their abstracts and OJS landing pages, not their full texts. The pricing block in facts.md is empty, so the post states nothing about cost anywhere, which leaves the reader's live question — what should I spend — unanswered. And the domain is far below the florists and marketplaces that own these ten results; ranking here is a matter of months and I am not predicting it.
